rv.q: Ireland is never merely gratuitous and has a genius for embarrassing moral dilemmas.
The turning of tables is riveting to watch.
The play dances to and fro, interweaving serious questions with crisply funny dialogue and combining the absurd with the profound.
The revised version at London’s Sohoplace is leaner and all the more compelling.
The play is perceptive about what it means to put your trust not just in another person but also in a programme or organised religion.
The dialogue is sharp and dynamic, full of snappy banter and brutal truths, and the slippery text keeps the audience continually guessing and reassessing the characters’ true motivations.
As it is, it’s a tight, thought-provoking, 85-minute vehicle for two actors at the top of their game.
Ireland’s script is witty and engaging, but the plot struggles to excite in the same way.
Still, it feels both softer and less purposeful than the plays that made Ireland’s name.
But it’s also funny, weird, well acted and provocative in a much more profound way than the nihilistic button pressing of old.
But the play itself remains a step-change short of a knock-out sensation.
This is an exceptionally well made, highly addictive drama.
A slight premise taken to amusing heights by performances that lift it to another level.
It is a privilege to watch two such accomplished actors deliver the goods in such an unfettered and exposed environment.
The Fifth Step, carefully directed by Finn den Hertog, spins through many moods and multiple questions but it never loses its grip.
Lowden, as is usual with this exceptional actor, totally inhabits this wired character, for once talking in his native Scots accent.
Scorching one-liners, usually delivered by a deadpan Lowden but sometimes a quick-to-bite Freeman, ensure the play remains surprisingly funny at every turn.
A searingly honest and darkly funny two-hander that grips from the first sip of black coffee to the final, devastating confession
When it comes to must-see plays in the West End at the moment, this is several steps ahead of the rest.
The newly reworked play is additionally a sophisticated, complex piece that interweaves difficult topics into a substantial, compelling and often surprising production.

cn.t: Ireland's darkly comic two-hander about AA mentorship earns praise for Lowden and Freeman's intense performances and searingly honest writing, though some critics find it less punchy than the playwright's earlier provocations.
